Demonstrative Pronouns Review
Demonstrative pronouns refer to nouns (objects, animals, people, etc.) that the speaker and the interlocutor clearly see; demonstrative pronouns show the distance between the speaker and the noun.

The demonstrative pronouns are This, That, These, and Those.

You can use this or these when you want to emphasize that something is near. Use this for singular nous and these for plural nouns.

Examples:
This is a mandatory field. (singular)
These are the parameters you have to validate. (plural)

You can use that or those to show that something is far. Use that for singular nous and those for plural nouns.

Examples:
That is the data validation process you have to perform. (singular)
Those are the most common errors that users make.(plural)

Infinitives of Purpose in Sentences with Be Going to.
Use the infinitive of purpose to express the reason why you are doing something.

Use be going to so as to refer to future plans that were planned prior speaking. You can also use the infinitive of purpose in order to show the reason why you are going to perform such action in the future.

Some basic rules you must take into account when using the infinitive of purpose may include the following:

The infinitive of purpose shows the reason why the subject of the sentence does what he/she does; therefore, if the subject is different from the one showing the purpose, you use “so that.”

Compare:
John is going to add some validity rules to the online forms to help users avoid making mistakes. (John will do, John will help).

John is going to add some validity rules to the online forms so that users avoid making mistakes. (John will do, someone else will avoid).

In more formal contexts or when you are using stative verbs (be, know, look, etc.), use in order to or so as to instead of to.

In order to know what kind of validity rules you are going to use, you need to know what the forms are for.

John is going to set some validity rules to the forms so as to be sure the forms are going to work well and users won't make any mistakes.

Remember that the negative form will always be in order NOT to…

compare:
John is going to set some security rules in order not to allow users access information they should not get.

John is not going to remove the validity rules of the form in order not to make things harder than they are.

images.text:
Mary: Ok, I think that's it; we are done with the online forms.
Martin: Not yet, in fact, we need to set some data validation rules so that people do not enter the wrong information in the fields. 
Mary: I see. What else are you going to do there? 
Martin: I'm just going to set 5 simple data validation rules to ensure the information we gather from users is clean. Here, let me show you how they work. 
This is the form level validation; this process is going to set some fields as mandatory to ensure the users mark all the checkboxes correctly; otherwise, they're not going to be able to move forward.

Mary: What's this other validation process for? 
Martin: That's the field level validation. That's going to play an important role in the web page to make sure the users enter the correct character values in a determined data field; that way, we can be sure there won't be human errors in our databases.
Similarly, I'm going to set the data saving and search criteria validation processes so that people can save their data and query results in case they want to change or close the page. 
Mary: Those two sound important. But, what about that one?

Martin: Ah, this is the range validation process. It is going to determine a specific range so that people do not enter data out of the parameters, such as future dates or invalid numbers. In my humble opinion, those five are the most important data validation processes. 
Mary: Ok, let me know when you finish so that I can tell the manager to come and check.
